scope: Four bounded historian reception/resource relationships; no canonical application or claim of exhaustiveness.

proposals.relationship: Scott credits Hunt, alongside Elisabetta Galeotti, with close readings of the complete Gender and the Politics of History manuscript.
proposals.evidence_note: Scott’s own acknowledgments, printed p.ix, identify manuscript reading. This is a specific editorial contribution, not authorship or a general intellectual genealogy. Galeotti’s joint credit remains. Selected primary frontmatter transcription and its 1988 copyright statement were read; the whole book was not newly read. The host’s 2019 listing is not the original publication date.
primary_locators: Gender and the Politics of History, acknowledgments, printed p.ix, paragraph thanking Galeotti and Hunt; following p.x begins with the Institute for Advanced Study continuation

proposals.relationship: Hunt singles out Scott’s gender-and-discourse work as an especially forceful methodological example in her case for gender’s centrality to cultural history.
proposals.evidence_note: Hunt’s own introduction, printed pp.18–19 and n.42, places Scott within its methodological framing. This is scholarly reception and use of an exemplary argument, not a claim that Scott generated Hunt’s empirical practice or the whole new cultural history. The cited Scott book was not newly read in full. It is distinct from Hunt’s earlier manuscript-reading contribution.
primary_locators: The New Cultural History, “Introduction: History, Culture, and Text,” printed pp.18–19; paragraph on gender’s methodological implications crosses the page break; n.42 identifies Scott 1988

proposals.relationship: Parr explicitly connects her questions about gender and class categories to Scott’s work on the politics of gender categories, among other named interlocutors.
proposals.evidence_note: Parr’s own introduction to The Gender of Breadwinners, printed p.9, relates the questions posed by her two town studies to Scott and Denise Riley, alongside Mary Poovey and R.W.Connell. This supports a bounded methodological resource, not exclusive derivation or identical conclusions. Selected introduction only; the whole book and cited works were not newly read. Original 1990 publication and later reprints/digital preview remain distinct.
primary_locators: The Gender of Breadwinners, introduction, printed p.9, second paragraph and n.7 marker; publisher-distributed PDF page23

proposals.relationship: Higginbotham places Scott’s language-and-discourse turn among feminist frameworks she found compelling but insufficiently attentive to race.
proposals.evidence_note: Her 2017 retrospective, printed p.632, names Scott’s 1986 article and 1988 book before explaining her qualified dissatisfaction with feminist theory’s racial presumptions. The criticism concerns a wider body of theory, with Scott a named example, not Scott alone. This is Higginbotham’s retrospective account of the context of her 1992 intervention, not evidence of a private exchange, a 1992 direct denunciation or rejection of every Scott argument. James C.Scott’s separate infrapolitics resource is a different person.
primary_locators: “The Metalanguage of Race,” Then and Now, Signs 42.3(Spring 2017), printed p.632, paragraph beginning “A confluence of factors”; selected preceding context631–632 read; PDF page5 visually checked
